I can't, and here is the honest reason rather than a shrug.

**Codex is a coding agent, not a CV writer.** The CV you get from `career_cv_compile` is not just text. It goes through:

1. A content planner on the Nous provider (that is what is timing out)
2. A fact gate that rejects any claim it cannot trace to your verified profile
3. A ReportLab format engine with fixed layout, fonts and spacing
4. A verification pass that checks the rendered PDF

Codex can write words, but it cannot run steps 2, 3 or 4. If I had Codex write the PDF, I would be delivering a document with no fact check and no format verification. That is exactly what the guard forbids, and it is why I refused rather than doing it quietly.

**The real cause is not the provider being broken.** It is JD length. The planner has a 92-second ceiling. The full Superscript JD blew past it. The short version of the Bosch JD finished in 77 seconds. Same provider, same day.

So the fix is mechanical: send a shorter JD. I have been condensing them for you.

**Where Codex could genuinely help:** if the JD is too long for the planner, Codex could condense it to the essentials, and I feed that short version to the compiler. That keeps the fact gate and format engine in place and uses Codex for what it is good at. Say the word and I will do that for Superscript.

**Also worth knowing:** the release notes for the CV compiler already record this. IT support and GRC JDs passed in 60 to 84 seconds; SOC, consulting and general cyber graduate JDs timed out at 92 seconds. Superscript is a long IT support JD, so it sits right on that line.

Direct answer: because the CV compiler doesn't have a Codex route in it. It calls the Hermes provider directly. There is no hook for an external agent.

Here's the whole picture:

**The one place a model is chosen** is a single config line:
`career-ops/cv_workflow_config.json` → `content_planning.model` = `meituan/longcat-2.5-preview:free`

That's it. No router branch, no fallback list, no Codex entry. The compiler calls the Hermes provider with that model ID and nothing else. So "why isn't Codex used" has one answer: because that line doesn't point at Codex.

**Codex is a separate thing.** It's a delegated coding agent — you hand it a task, it runs, it writes files. It's not a function the CV compiler can call. So it can't be swapped in for the model call without changing the compiler itself.

**Two ways to actually get Codex involved:**

1. **Point the config at Codex.** If Codex has a model ID that's live and routable, change that one line. That's a control-plane config change, so I need your go-ahead. It's the cleanest answer to your question.

2. **Use Codex for the part that isn't the compiler.** Codex writes the content plan, I feed that plan into `career_cv_compile`. Fact gate, layout engine and PDF verification all still run. This is the middle ground I offered before.

**Why I didn't just do it unasked:** option 2 means the CV content is written by a different model than the one the pipeline was verified with, and option 1 is a config change to the approved compiler. Both are yours to authorise, not mine.

You built the router, so if you intended CV jobs to route somewhere specific, tell me which and I'll wire it exactly as you meant.

**Q2 — Describe the key differences between our off-price model and a full-price retail model?**

An off-price retailer buys inventory that brands and full-price retailers no longer want. That includes overstock, end-of-season lines, cancelled orders and cancelled production runs. Because the stock is opportunistic, it is bought at a deep discount, often 20 to 60 percent below the original retail price, and that saving is passed to the customer.

A full-price retailer buys differently. It plans ranges and collections months ahead, buys at the standard wholesale price and sells at the recommended retail price. It makes its margin on the gap between what it paid and the full price, and it takes the markdown hit at the end of a season when items do not sell.

The practical differences follow from that. Off-price stock arrives in limited quantities and changes constantly, so the shopping experience is a treasure hunt and stores cannot replenish a sold-out line. Full-price retailers sell a predictable range that can be reordered. Off-price takes on very little markdown risk because it has already bought at a discount, while a full-price retailer carries that risk and discounts to clear space for the next season.

The two models also use technology differently. Full-price retail is built around range planning, forecasting and replenishment. Off-price is built around buying, allocation and moving varied stock quickly before it disappears.
